utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, The Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, good afternoon. You may notice from the proofing notes and from the statements, there's something I just wanted to give a little background on. I've had a chance to briefly speak to Mr. Karnavas about it, as it mainly deals with that part of the case. And it has to do with protective measures and what exhibits should be under seal. This -- in fact, could we go into private session at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can move into open session, Your Honours. I just would like to ask before we start to question this witness, this is an administrative matter, we were planning to return to Bosnia tomorrow, and we have our plane tickets booked due to some obligations we have out in the field. However, in our conversation with Mr. Karnavas, there is the possibility that this will not be finished today. If this is to be the case, that would mean that we would have to postpone our departure for Monday. So if you would permit us during the break to deal with these administrative matters with the Registry so that they could postpone our flight and put it off until Tuesday. I think this would be the last opportunity to do so, because it's Friday and I think the Registry is working only until 4.00 or perhaps 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, do I anticipate finishing today. Of course, we heard some additional information. And given this additional information and Court's ruling, obviously I'm going to make sure that we finish today. And if I need to go into areas, in other areas which would prolong it, I will reserve those for another day. And of course, those will be issues that will be of minor nature so it would not impact on the case itself. Because I do realise that Mr. Blagojevic does have a family visit, and we wanted to wrap this up. So I will do everything I possibly can to finish today, and I'll leave it at that. I anticipate the witness is going to be forthcoming, and I don't anticipate Mr. McCloskey taking too long. But there is a lot of material that I want to cover, and I will cover it in a rapid space of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will do our best to finish this witness today. And I hope nobody will have a dinner party tonight as we may sit a little bit longer so to wrap up the case. Yes, could we have the witness please. For the sake of the record, I would like to say that Judge Argibay won't be able to be with us today. The remaining Judges decided to continue the proceedings in accordance with Rule 15(B). This is just for the sake of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. I want to show you a piece of paper and ask you if this is your name. But before that, can you just tell us -- I don't need your date of birth -- but how old are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I'm 55. Yes, that is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is Exhibit Number 206, Your Honour. Sorry, that's 475. And could you briefly outline where you grew up and what your initial education was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I grew up in the village in which I was born, in the Municipality of Gradiska in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I completed the military academy after completing secondary school. It's the command staff academy. So I became a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what year was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: When I completed the academy, it was in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you became -- became a professional soldier with the -- at that time JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just very briefly describe your career as it led up until the outbreak of the war in Bosnia, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: My first post was in Slovenia, the Republic of Slovenia, until 1988. Then I served in Belgrade in the centre of the high military academies as a trainer in the inner military academy class. In 1993, on the 8th of January, I was ordered to report to the Army of Republika Srpska, and that is where I spent a period of my career, right until I went -- until my retirement, in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you retire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: On the 28th of February 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At what rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session briefly for some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at some point in July of 1995, did you receive any orders relating to the operation to -- related to the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. I did receive an order that from the brigade composition, I should set aside certain troops which would be the equivalent of a battalion, a battalion-strong unit that in structure there would be various specialties, and that I should be ready to go into action in the area between the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves. And that was at the end of June and the beginning of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you receive any order to go to a particular place around that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The order was that those men, the provisional formation, should go to the area of Zelani Jadar, and Jasenova, which is a smaller village, and that they should put up there and wait further orders and assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What about yourself? Did you personally receive an order to go someplace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was supposed to report. I saw the unit off. I saw that formation off, and I reported to the command post of the Bratunac Brigade in Bratunac itself. And that was the 5th of July, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened at the Bratunac Brigade on the 5th of July when you went there? You need to speak up. I don't think anyone heard you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a meeting of officers related to the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, at that command post which I suppose was the forward command post of the Drina Corps, everyone, including me, all the officers who were supposed to receive assignments and take part in the operation, reported to the commander of the operation there, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us just briefly what instructions the people that were at this meeting received that day? This would be the 5th of July at the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: On that day, assignments were given for individual axes of involvement, engagement for the units, the way in which they -- sanitary and medical protection was to be provided, firepower protection -- preparation for the offensive, and other activities that were linked to logistics, to reconnoitering and reconnaissance, and everything that is generally taken in situations of this kind, and preparedness for the launch of the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I don't want to get into the details of the operation at this point, but did you take part in the operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the 11th of July, did you actually have the opportunity to go into the town of Srebrenica with other soldiers and officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have a brief clip, but we should play that in private session, if we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. What's the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can answer that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In private session. Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, about what time did you go back to your base there and do these basic things to get -- to get your -- to get straightened up, straightened away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I stayed with the unit while it was still daylight. And when it became dark, I was already at Jasenova at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go anywhere that evening? Did you leave the command post at Jasenova?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, I didn't go anywhere. I had dinner and went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you get any communications or any information about any meetings in Bratunac or anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Not before I went to bed. However, in the morning I think it was, when I woke up --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This would be now the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, the 12th of July, in the morning, at breakfast time or just after I awoke, the signalsman conveyed to me the information that came out from the command post asking me to report to the region of the repeater station, and I think that was for 9.00 or 10.00. I think it was for 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just describe to us where this location was. I don't think we need a map, if you can just describe to us how close it was to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: About 2 or 3 kilometres. It's a curve, there's a curve there with this repeater station, which is visible, up on an elevation, and that's where I reported to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is that elevation called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Bojna, or Rijina. I think it was Bojna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so did you go there and meet General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time did you meet General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I think it was 9.00. And he didn't greet me separately, but I went up to report to him. He -- Colonel Vicic issued assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us just briefly who Vicic is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Colonel Vicic was the operations man, the operations officer in the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And briefly, what were your orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: My unit's assignment pursuant to those orders was to search the area from Srebrenica through the village of Viogora towards a facility at Jahorina. It was a mountain facility called Jahorina. The right-flank communication, viewing it from Srebrenica towards Derventa, I believe. So that was my daily assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you carry that out that day, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I carried that assignment out, and I arrived with my unit. We were -- had infantry men and reconnoitering men, and the deployment was on a regular basis. We spread out to search the terrain. And we moved towards the facility and performed the assignment sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And sometime that afternoon, did you receive communication to do something, to meet someone somewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. At around 1800 hours, I was told to return to the first houses at the village of Viogora on the road there and to report there to General Krstic who was waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. I arrived. I went back and met up with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At what time did you meet the General?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I've already said that that was about 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I reported to him how far the unit had come, what I saw, and he conveyed to me -- or rather, he gave me the task that at night, at 2100 hours, I was to be at the command post, or rather the forward command post of the Drina Corps at Bratunac, at the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he give you any other information about why you were to report to the Bratunac Brigade that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you report to the Bratunac Brigade that evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course, I did. And I arrived there at 2100 hours. I obeyed orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what route did you drive from the area where you were around Srebrenica to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I took the route, or rather, I went back to the Srebrenica settlement and took the road leading to Srebrenica via Potocari, Bratunac, and I passed there with my vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say you arrived at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at about 2100 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what you were able to see when you drove through Potocari shortly before that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Along the road en route, there was movement on the part of the civilian population, but in Potocari there was a general mass of people, people were assembling. There was a crowd. There were vehicles. People were loading up. There was the civilian and military police regulating traffic, the passage of vehicles and people. I assumed that some food supplies were coming in. But I didn't stop. I just passed through, taking the road through the settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you saw military police. How do you know they were military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Judging by their uniforms that they wore, and the cross belts that the police wore. It was obvious that this was the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What colour were the belts that you saw these people wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: White.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were the military police doing that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: At the time that I passed by, I had the impression that they were maintaining order, so that the road would be kept clear since there was such a mass of people there. So to make sure that the road was clear, that passage was clear. I don't know. They probably had some other assignments, allocation, recordkeeping, but I don't know who was doing what and what their assignments were when I was passing along that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us an idea roughly what time it was when you went through Potocari.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It was still daylight. It wasn't dark yet. It was summertime, the 12th of July. I had to be in Bratunac at 9.00, so it was about 8.30 or a quarter to 9.00. I think that that was about the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any memory of how many different military police officers you saw there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what unit those military police officers were from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you got to the Bratunac Brigade command, where did you go in the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I went to the operations room, to the duty officer. Each command post had a duty officer in the operations room. And I asked him where I was supposed to report to, where the meeting would be held. So he directed me to the room where the meeting was to be held.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who did you go with, if anyone, to the Bratunac Brigade command from your command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No one came along. It was just me and the driver to that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what did you do and who did you see after checking in with the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I went to that room. The others were there, the other officers who had received the same assignment as myself. We talked, greeted each other. I think that we reported on the situation in the units and on the problems that we were burdened with since it was already the seventh or the eighth day that we were in that area, outside of our area -- home-base area, private area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to private session again, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You had mentioned that Mladic had arrived at the Bratunac Brigade at about 10.00 and described some of the things that you recall him saying. How long did that period last where the people like yourself were gathered there listening to General Mladic and discussing the things you've talked to us about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I cannot tell you precisely for how long, but I think it was less than an hour. The meeting was short with specific tasks issued. I don't remember any other discussions in particular. There was a dinner organised afterwards in the room or the facility which served as a restaurant in that building. So from the arrival of myself until General Mladic came and until the dinner, I don't think that this -- all of this took longer than two or two and a half hours. So I assume that the meeting was not long.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So after the meeting, there was a dinner. Were there any speeches at the dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The dinner was a purely military affair, if I can put it that way, not much conversation or discussion about assignments or any specific conversations generally. It was a short dinner held in a separate room, not in the dining hall, a self-service dining hall. We were actually served dinner by the cooks or whoever, the staff serving dinner in the restaurant generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But was General Mladic at this dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was -- who else was at the dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The same people who were at the meeting, General Krstic and the rest, the others who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any new people in addition to those that attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall anything significant, any significant information you received at that dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go -- what did you do after the dinner?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: You mean me personally?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: After dinner, I took the opportunity to use a telephone, a fixed telephone line to call my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: After that, I went to my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember about what time you left the brigade that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I went from the brigade. I left the brigade, or to the brigade. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time did you leave the Bratunac Brigade that evening after dinner and the phone call?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I understand. Well, I arrived there a little after midnight, at about 12.30. I arrived at my command post, and it took me half an hour or 45 minutes. So that means that I left at about half past 11.00 or quarter to 12.00. That was when I left the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you go through Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you see, if anything, in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't think I saw anything. I slept or dozed. I was very tired. I had been working the whole day, so I dozed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The next morning, can you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The next morning, I gathered up my unit since the order was that around 10.00 in the region of the village of Vijogora, General Mladic would address my troops, so I went to the area, gathered up my men in order to be able to report and to welcome General Mladic and General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: General Mladic addressed the fighters. He congratulated them, and he told them of their new assignment to which this part of my unit was to be assigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did General Krstic say anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't think so. The soldiers heard what he said, they accepted it, they got into their own vehicles and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It was my task to organise a march to the next region from which the unit, that particular composition of the unit, was to be deployed and engaged. And that's what I did. I issued assignments, issued assignments with regard to security for transport vehicles, and I started off after seeing off my men into a column. I also moved towards the broader region around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what route the men took and what route you took.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The unit took, or rather, when everything had been prepared, the unit took the direction taking it across Derventa and the bauxite mines, and then the main road at Milici. And then from Vlasenica, Han Pijesak to the region of Zepa. The broader region around the Zepa, or rather the area that was designated for us to reach and report to. And I set off in my own vehicle through Srebrenica up to Bratunac, where I had lunch in that same dining hall, the self-service area this time, and continued on my journey to the same area to meet up with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember - this would be on the 13th of July - about what time you went through Potocari on your way to Bratunac and then on to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon. I arrived in the area of Krivaca or Kusici - I can't quite remember the name - at around 1900 our 2000 hours. So that is five or six hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you see when you went through Potocari that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: In Potocari, there was a mass of people. They were loading up, boarding various vehicles. There were buses there, and trucks. And my own vehicle, once I had passed by, made up the column of these vehicles conducting the evacuation. So I was in that same column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, on the 13th, did you see any VRS troops in the area of Potocari when you went through?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I think they were the policemen, both military and civilian, who were seeing to law and order during the loading. And you had to introduce a bit of order because not everybody could get on at the same time, all at once. So they were there to see to that. And then along the road, you would see a soldier here and there or a policeman at intervals. And I suppose there were the curious, too, who perhaps didn't have an assignment but who were just there to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In Potocari, you said you think that there were policemen and military police. Is there some doubt in your mind of what you saw there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, there were. They were there to see to law and order, and they were conducting the boarding. They would make groups of people, and they were present while these people were boarding. But they were there to see that everything was in order. Yes, they were there, and they provided security and free passage, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "they," who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Those same people, the policemen whose job it was generally speaking to see that the roads were kept free, that people didn't jam the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "policemen," can you be more specific, what kind of policemen? We know there's military police, there's civilian police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: There were both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us any kind of an estimate of how many military policemen you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: On that short section of road, there weren't more than 10 to 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And civilian police -- when you say "short section of road" what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Where the facility was, whether it was a company, an enterprise of some sort, and the parking lot belonging to that company. So one or two hundred metres around that where the crowds of people were mostly located, and on the other side the vehicles would be parked and the people would board the vehicles there, on the opposite side of the road. So there were the people on one side, the transport vehicles on the other. So in boarding the vehicles, that's where the policemen were, to see that all this was done in order, so they were seeing to that area. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, you say "policemen." Can you tell us which policemen, or again, if it's both, were there to supervise the boarding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Well, believe me when I say I don't know. I passed by and saw that they were there. Some of them were on the left-hand side; the others were on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think you say around -- is it 10 or 15 military police? Can you give us an estimate of civilian police in the same area at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you see any Muslim men being separated from the crowd of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Apart of the area where I passed by in my vehicle, and we were driving at about 30 kilometres per hour, didn't actually allow me to assess something like that. I just passed by, passed along the road, and didn't notice anything vital except to see that there were one and there were the others and they were boarding the vehicles. Some vehicles had already left, so I just -- we just drove in the column. And that's more or less how it was. We drove behind them until Bratunac. So I found myself in this column. There was a truck in front of me with people in it, women and children. We didn't wave to each other, but of course I could see who was on the truck and who was doing the transporting. I don't know what was happening behind me, but there was a truck of these people. They were men and women and children, some women were older, others were younger. Young men. As I say, there were a lot of people in that truck. I couldn't see those further ahead of me in the column or behind me in the column. Just this one truck in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You say you stopped at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I had lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Commander Blagojevic when you checked into his brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. Objection. He never said that he checked into the headquarters. He went there for lunch. There is a distinction. So I just -- I want to make sure that he's not checking in. Now he can ask him, Did you check in? There's a difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, you may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see Commander Blagojevic when you went to the brigade headquarters for lunch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you make any effort to check in with him or identify that you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, I didn't look for him. I just went to the duty officer in the operations room to ask him where I could have lunch. And I was told that I could go into the dining hall, the one that they used otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was in the headquarters building, the dining hall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, in the headquarters building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any officers or soldiers of any units that you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you just had lunch and then left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I had lunch and left, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember about what time you left the Bratunac Brigade headquarters that afternoon? This would be now the 13th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that was the 13th of July, and I've already said that I arrived in the region between 1900 and 2000 hours. I don't know what time it was exactly, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well I -- I know what time you got to Zepa. But can you help us on what time you would have left the Bratunac Brigade headquarters? Because we're not as familiar. We know it may have been a difficult drive that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Well, let's say it was around 1700 and 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, from the drive from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, did you see anything of significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any groupings of Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Around Konjevic Polje, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Or between Bratunac and Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about from Konjevic Polje on towards Milici? Did you see anything of significance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In the settlement called Nova Kasaba on the playground or stadium -- in the playground, I saw some men who had been assembled there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were those -- what kind of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Men sitting on the football field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was this a football field -- how big was the football field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know the exact dimensions, but like any other ordinary football field. It wasn't a top league that this team from this small place played in, but generally that was the size.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So it wasn't a tiny children's football field; it was a football field that adults played football on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, it was an adults' football field used by the Kasaba team, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were these Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I assume so because they were along the road, and there was some military police there providing security, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How much of the football field was covered with these men sitting as you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I think the whole field was covered with men sitting down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And after that, did you go on to the -- to the area of the Zepa operations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you stop anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. Rather, no. I did not stop anywhere until the designated spot which was where the unit was to be deployed from which it was to go on further on assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then did you continue in the Zepa activities on the following day, the 14th, through other days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now I want to take you back to a -- I believe you met with me and an investigator, Ken Corlett on the 21st of January 2002. Do you recall having a diary of events from that time period with you then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you take some notes out of that diary that you provided for us at the time about some of the important days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I could show you a photocopy of something, I want you to -- it should be Exhibit 474. And if you could just show the B/C/S version. Do you recognise the handwriting on those notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, it's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you write down those notes from your actual diary that day you met with us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. Based on my diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about your diary, when the events in it were filled out and what purpose you used it for.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Since -- in view of the tasks I was given and my participation or my unit's participation in the assignment, every night I would write in the basics, the basic events that took place that day. I'd write that down in my diary, the ones I took part in, the outlines. And the object of keeping a diary like that was just to keep a record of what was going on and perhaps this gave me an opportunity to put pen to paper and put it all down in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so this -- these pieces of paper that are in front of you now, did you write those down as you reviewed your original diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. I wrote it down in chronological order as corresponded to the diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't think I will ask you to go over those details. But just to say, are those details that you've written down and given to us reflect correctly the entries in your original diary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just want to start a little bit by asking you some background information. In particular, as I understand it from hearing you, you spent approximately five years teaching at the military academy in Belgrade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask what exactly you were teaching, what subjects or at what level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I taught in the tactics department. I taught artillery tactics at the military academy for a year and a half. And from 1990, 1st of September, I was the chief or the head of the class of the military academy which came to the academy of that year. That was the 47th class to the academy. And then from that post, I was transferred to duty in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it in teaching, you were -- you had to refer to the rules and regulations on occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Not occasionally; as much as possible in any case. I did not want to omit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And so I take it that you're pretty familiar with the rules and the regulations specifically as they might relate to the corps or to brigades. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it it has been some time since you've taught. And as I understand it, you're in retirement. But would it be fair to say that you still remember the rules or understand them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Is that a question, or my personal position, or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My question is, if I were to ask you about the rules --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I were to ask you concretely about the rules of the corps, could we have a discussion on them? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: We can discuss it if I can, if I'm able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's my question. Because of the passage of time, you're not teaching and you're out of the profession, do you still recall the rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course, I remember that. But it's not something that I deal with on a daily basis. But in view of my experience, I am even -- I even avoid talking about them now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it if we wanted to discuss the brigade rules, given your past experience, you will probably be even more familiar with not just what's on paper but also what was -- how they applied in practice. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Please do not make me draw conclusions. Just ask what you're interested in knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how am I asking you to draw a conclusion? I'm simply asking you whether you are able, capable, perhaps even willing to discuss the brigade rules given your previous position and experience in the field.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your position, did you have a zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, was that zone of responsibility based on the rules, the brigade rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: In this case, no. The area was much broader than the brigades would be assigned to in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, having looked at the rules and discussed the rules extensively here in court, we have not been able to find anywhere in the rules anything that specifies that a brigade has a zone of responsibility. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: A brigade is, in the implementation of its tasks, is given a zone or area of defence. As we mainly held defensive positions, specifically this brigade, this brigade carried out tasks of a defensive nature, and we could say that that was its area of its responsibility. Everything that happens as a rule in a defensive area or area of defence, everything that happens in that quadrant or in those facilities in accordance with the depth and width of the area is called area of responsibility, all the things that happen within the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So your understanding is that's the area of responsibility. Would that be similar to saying that's the zone of defence? Am I using the correct terminology?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I think that you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Would that -- if I were to use the term "zone of operation," would that be similar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, you could consider it to be the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you are to look at the Bratunac Brigade zone, we know that they were -- you had the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Battalion. They were lined in a particular geographical area. If I understand you correctly, what you're telling us is that their zone of operation or zone of defence would have entailed a certain width, a certain depth. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked to put together a battalion in order to join in the operation, the attack of Srebrenica. Was that battalion operating in the zone of operation or zone of defence of the Bratunac Brigade as you understand those terms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And if I understand you correctly, the Bratunac Brigade was not one of your neighbours during the attack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No. With your permission, may I just be allowed to say the following: The attack in the direction of the Srebrenica settlement as a term in this specific operation, after the regrouping of units, and this happened on the 10th or rather the 11th -- on the morning of the 11th, the assignments were changed for my unit. It was moved to the right, to the northwesterly reaches above the town. Up until then, there was no talk of an attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. The initial operation was to separate even more the two enclaves, Zepa and Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. And to narrow down the enclaves, in view of the events that took place before the decision in which I participated with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when you say "the events," we're talking about where members of the 28th Division under the protection of the UN while in Srebrenica would leave the enclave and would commit atrocities against the Serb villages surrounding that area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, there's no occasion that the UN is protecting Naser Oric in his attacks. That's a little theatrical at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 28th Division was inside -- was inside Srebrenica and certainly they made no effort to completely demilitarise that enclave as they were required to, and this had been ongoing for many years. So I don't think there's any dispute here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Karnavas, I think you should put your questions strictly to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, you're referring to the attacks by the 28th, members of the 28th Division going out and committing atrocities outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: From the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and then as you indicated, at some point when it appeared that there was very little resistance, if any, that the possibility of taking over Srebrenica was a reality, the orders shifted. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then we see on the -- on July 11th, we see members of the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we hear the B/C/S. I think it's the wrong channel. Mr. Karnavas, can you try it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then on the 11th, we see certain members, officers of the VRS, in Srebrenica as a result of it falling. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: When Srebrenica fell, as far as you knew, it was still a mystery as to where members of the 28th Division actually were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In other words, if you didn't come across the 28th Division when you got to Srebrenica -- and we know that they weren't in Potocari. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Me personally, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You and the other VRS officers. We're talking about the 11th now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, we didn't know where they were. It was assumed that they had taken to the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you being on the ground there, can you tell us when you first became aware as to where they might be located or in which direction they're headed toward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The members of the BH army, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Well, I think that on the basis of the order to secure the roads that we were supposed to pass through towards Tuzla and Kladanj, those roads, that line of communication, we assumed that they wouldn't go to the south in view of the fact that the forces in securing the enclave were there. I don't know when I learned of this exactly, but it was the conclusion of every officer that they wanted to join up with their own forces in the other area, the Tuzla/Kladanj area, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the -- after the fall of Srebrenica on the 11th, that afternoon and evening, where did you spend it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: After the fall of Srebrenica, I was in my own unit while it was daylight, during the day, to organise security on the line we had reached, to deploy units along the line, and to establish contacts with our neighbours. And after that, I went to my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how far was your command post from there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Not far. I can't tell you exactly now. But not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it that you gave -- go ahead. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It's -- from Srebrenica, you pass the repeater station, and then Zelani Jadar, and then up again, up a hill. But the road was an asphalt one, so it didn't take you long to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the battalion that you put together, how many men approximately were under your command when you led this mission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: About 300, perhaps a little more. But approximately 300 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you tell us, were you able during that period of time to know where every one of those 300 men were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Not every single man, but where the officers and their groups were, it was normal for me to know which region they were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it that after the fall of Srebrenica when you went to visit your officers, one of the reasons was to give them some instructions as to what to do. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: When I arrived at the command post, or rather when I had left the Srebrenica settlement, then, is that what you mean? What period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That period. That period. The fall of -- Srebrenica has fallen. I take it that you must have visited or contacted your officers to let them know what to do next, which might have been do nothing, hold your positions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No. I've already said that I went to the unit and issued assignments for the night, what they should do, how they should organise themselves. And when everything was made clear to them, I went to my command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we know that there was a lot of looting in Srebrenica after it fell. And I believe one of the terms that you use for folks that might have gone -- some of the folks that were in Potocari were "the curious." Do you know for certain whether any of your soldiers on their own, without instructions, might have been one of those that either looted or just were curious and went off on their own just to take a look? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: There were such men, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Not that any orders were given; in fact, the orders were probably the opposite, to maintain their positions. But nonetheless, from experience, as you well know, some individuals sometimes do not follow orders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Correct, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, just to be absolutely certain, on July 11th, that evening, okay, this is the day that Srebrenica fell, that evening, you were not at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you did not attend any meetings that particular night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution has argued repeatedly before this Trial Chamber that their theory is that on the night of the 11th to the 12th, sometime during that period --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but using "the Prosecution's theory" to present an -- a witness is absolutely improper. There's ways of getting to any factual question, but pitting him against the Prosecution in some sort of personal way is just not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey is a little sensitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we are under time constraint. Just put your question directly, and we'll take whatever the witness answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm doing my best. I'm doing my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It has been argued --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is absolutely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me -- I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, rephrase it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From the night -- during night of the 11th, between the night of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, did you and other Serb officers, Mladic, Krstic, Andric and the others, get together and plan to execute and kill all the Muslim men from age 16 to 60?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That misstates anything that has been in the record. Nobody has ever suggested this officer was involved in any plot. And the impression this leaves is, again, trying to make it personal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yeah, but this time, you know, Mr. Karnavas did not indicate who put up this kind of theory. He just asked a question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But he's assuming that this person is involved in such a plot. There's no fact in evidence that suggests that. And so it cannot -- it's not a fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe on Mr. Karnavas' part. Do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could -- if we could just rewind the tape back to yesterday where we heard the Prosecution express what they believe happened and when it happened, and that this idea occurred sometime between the night of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, and that there is a clear distinction. Might I also remind the Trial Chamber that there was a specific question asked of this witness with regard to whether he saw anything on his way to Zepa on the 13th. I think that I'm entitled -- they opened the door. First of all, I'm entitled to ask him whether he participated in any meeting. That's the first question. Second question, does he know of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, just ask the question whether this witness took part in any meeting on the 11th at night. If the witness's answer is yes, then ask the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I see. Thank you, Your Honour. I see. We'll go step by step. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you attend any meetings on the night of the 11th, between the night of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, I should like to ask you that once you hear my answer to give me a chance to rest for a bit. Take a rest. My answer is no, I did not part in any meeting during the night, or rather, in the night between the 11th and the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll take a rest. We're about ready for a break anyway. So if there's any time you want a break, you tell us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a 20-minute break. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, sir, let's talk about the 12th of July. Okay? Now, on the morning of the 12th, as I understand it, you were given a particular task by General Krstic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And part of -- that order --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it that was an oral order, not written?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you indicated that you're not certain who else was present or who else received the order, but you recall the location where it was when you received that order. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that location is Bojna? If you could pronounce it for us.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Bojna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Bojna.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And how far is Bojna from the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. How long would it take to drive there under the conditions back then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: To be honest, I didn't live in the area, and I don't know. I don't know how many kilometres it is from Vlasenica to Srebrenica, but it's near Srebrenica anyway. It all depends. I really don't know. Half an hour, perhaps a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, what time exactly was it that General Krstic came by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: On the 12th in the morning, the tasks were set by Colonel Vicic. General Krstic, I think, was there when we reported in that locality. But the tasks were set by Colonel Vicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it tasked at that particular location? Is that where you received the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you -- if you recall what time it might have been in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Before noon anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it, since you were going to be searching the terrain, that you must have been given coordinates on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: They didn't give us coordinates, but the general axis for the units' engagement and the boundaries for the roads. I was supposed to take the right-hand side across the village of Vijogora towards the Jahorina facility. Geographically speaking, this was called Jahorina. And on my left was the 1st Birac Brigade, so to the left of that road to break through the Jastrebaca facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you have a neighbour on your right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't remember. I didn't establish contact with anybody on that side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you given a particular location that you had to reach by the end of the day, on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I just said, Jahorina was the destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So as soon as you reached that point, you were supposed to stop and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I take it from listening to your testimony, you're not aware whether any other brigades that might have been involved in the attack on Srebrenica were also issued, other than the ones that you've mentioned, were also issued orders to search?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't remember. But I know that I was given the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And of course --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: And that, if I might be allowed to finish, that the Zvornik Brigade, I think, was tasked to remain in reserve. Whether it sent a part of its force out to search, I don't really know. But that's what I can say for sure. As to the rest, the others, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you don't know given the line the -- the zone of operation or zone of defence of the Bratunac Brigade, you don't know whether on that particular day the commander of the Bratunac Brigade was also given oral orders to have his troops advance, searching the terrain, up to a certain point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Without asking you to speculate, given the circumstances on the ground, would you expect such an order to be also given to the Bratunac Brigade in light of their location and in light of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at some point on that particular day, you were informed that you had to make yourself available at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade at 2100 hours. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, you were told exactly the purpose for that meeting. In other words, you were told that you -- to go there because a meeting would be held. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: To come to a meeting, but I wasn't told what was to be discussed, just to report there at 2100 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: On that particular day, sir, was it your impression that the Bratunac Brigade headquarters was serving as the forward command post for the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what gave you that impression, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Because the first assignment and the first assembly with respect to the task around the enclaves was given to me at the headquarters of the Bratunac Brigade. And I'm quite sure that that was the forward command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are we speaking of the orders that you received on July 5, 1995? When you say the first orders you received, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we know that General Mladic was in the area. And we also know that some of his officers were also in the area, on or about those days, and I'm talking about after the fall of Srebrenica. Do you know whether the Bratunac Brigade also served as a forward command post for General Mladic when he was in that location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I can only assume because he arrived that day to that locality and issued certain tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I know this may sound like a silly question. But would General Mladic or General Krstic have to get permission from Colonel Blagojevic to use his headquarters as their forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: According to hierarchy, I don't think. It is the superior who can regulate matters that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And knowing General Mladic the way you knew him, and we can see some of his charismatic behaviour on tape, was General Mladic the type that would request the commander of the Bratunac Brigade's permission to use his facilities or even to order any of his men to carry out any tasks he thought needed to be done on the spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: That's a complex question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Could you simplify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you think General Mladic would -- given the personality that he was, was he the type that would go up to Colonel Blagojevic and ask him for permission to use his headquarters as his forward command post?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I'm going to resort to what I taught when I taught tactics and what I recommended to future officers and higher, advanced students. I don't think there was any need, and I don't think there is a need for a superior in combat operations, in operations generally, to request something of somebody. But that he regulates where he's going to develop his action, with respect to the infrastructure, the communications available, the roads available, how to communicate with his headquarters and his units in the field. And that he can regulate this by issuing orders, so that he can use that command post and the superior command in order to realise his role in the area, if I have been clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I take it given your answer that that would also apply to General Krstic or General Zivanovic when they were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And just while we're on the topic, we had a discussion here in this court on the concept of functional relationships as they are noted in the rules. Are you familiar with that concept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it if the chief of the rear services or the head of the rear services of the Drina Corps, for instance, were to ask the assistant commander of the rear services of the brigade, the Bratunac Brigade, to carry out a function that is within, within the rear services, that would be possible, would it not, without having to actually go and seek permission first from the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible. But he is duty-bound, that is to say, the assistant of that subordinated unit who has been tasked to inform his commander on the assignment he is using the men and resources for, or anything else, so that he would be able -- the commander would be able follow developments and to avoid having him placed in a situation to try and do something else whereas the assistant for the rear has already assigned a portion of men to somebody who requested him to do that, with the proviso that I'm quite sure that the assistant for the rear can, down the chain of command, suggest and say that he hasn't got enough men available. So he doesn't have to carry out everything literally as was requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I take it that principle would apply if, for instance, as you have the Bratunac Brigade headquarters serving as the forward command post of the Drina Corps, where you have General Krstic, who is the head of the Drina Corps there, the commander of the Drina Corps, and his assistant commander for rear services, if they're all located in the Bratunac Brigade headquarters working out of there, that principle would apply, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Hypotheticals need to have some basis in fact. I don't believe General Krstic was ever at the Bratunac Brigade when he was commander. He didn't become commander until he went to Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas. It's a hypothetical question, you know. In this situation, it's not proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Okay, Your Honours. I'm confused a little bit, though, because I thought on the 13th the Prosecution has argued that General Krstic has become commander because we have some orders. But I'll back off on that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back on the 12th, you arrive at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters on time, as you were ordered to do so. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And having searched your memory because you were questioned once in 2000, another time in 2002, again yesterday, and now today, you only recall certain personalities being there, certain officers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for those that you've indicated that were there for sure, you're certain about. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it one of the reasons is because you had an opportunity to observe them, perhaps talk to them, hear them, and maybe even break bread with them, eat with them later on. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the assumption or presumption that you've always made is that Colonel Blagojevic would have been there also since these were his headquarters. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So in a sense, even though they were now serving as a forward command post of the Drina Corps and perhaps the Main Staff, Colonel Blagojevic was still the host in a sense, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as a host commander, you would expect him to greet you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Perhaps in this case, it was a little bit different. We dropped by. I was personally told - I'm not speaking on behalf of the others - where the meeting would be held, in which room. The meeting was not held in the room where it would be logical, where the command -- the brigade commander would sit. Since him, if he were at this meeting, and this was an assumption, it's not an assertion because the assumption is that all the brigade commanders, just like myself, were supposed to attend the meeting, then he was also supposed to be up there. The room was up on the floor. So he should have been in that room or in front of the room. I don't remember particularly greeting each individual present, and I do not wish to say whether this person or that person was here or who sent whom, but I know that Pandurevic was there because we both asked a question, and that is why this is not something that I am doubting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: In relation to Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I was merely asking the question because given the culture, it's normally customary to, when you walk into somebody's command post or house, to greet them and maybe even make a little small talk, and especially if you're going to be having dinner with them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: In this case, yes, it was customary for this to happen. But the situation was such that we were supposed to go to a certain room where the meeting was supposed to be held. And so in this case, customary things were or could have been ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. At least there; certainly not at the dinner later on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The dinner was as dinner was. The seats were empty. We filled them. We were given dinner. There was some conversation. Most often the conversation was about the problems that we were dealing with. We were talking as we were eating, what was it that we were having troubles with as we were preparing for this assignment. This was not planned before. It was expected -- I personally expected that once we had completed the tasks, we would return to our own areas in order to carry out tasks in our areas. So this is what the conversation was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if at that meeting that took place on the evening of the 12th an argument had taken place between General Krstic and Colonel Blagojevic in front of General Mladic where there were complaints lodged against Colonel Blagojevic's men, the Bratunac Brigade, and the argument got so heated that Colonel Blagojevic walked out of both commanders, Mladic and Krstic, would that be an event that would stick in your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I assume that it would. But I don't recall anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Whether it's just a question of having forgotten, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you forget if there was a -- if there was an argument of such a nature on the 12th where a colonel would walk out in front of Mladic and Krstic out of protest, certainly that would be a significant event that would stick in your mind, would it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I've already said that I don't remember any other details from that meeting, other than these two or three that I actually noted down as something that was important to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we've had testimony here that -- from a driver that was with Mr. -- Colonel Blagojevic on that particular day who indicated that it was after 10.00 p.m., 2200 hours, that they arrived in Bratunac Brigade on the 12th. Might that explain why when you arrived at 2100 hours that particular evening Colonel Blagojevic wasn't there and doesn't stick in your mind as being there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It's just an assumption of mine. But I don't know everything about the persons that I noted and whom I believe were there at the time or took part in something. Everything else is just a question of speculation or assumption, of course as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we've also heard testimony that while -- that on this particular day, Colonel Blagojevic went and inspected some of his troops. Given the circumstances of what had just happened, that is, on the 11th, would you expect the brigade commander in that particular area as one of his functions to be visiting his troops, ensuring that everything was in proper order and perhaps even giving orders such as the ones that you had received?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course, just as I and the others after each task had to report -- had to convey this to our subordinates, and then go out and see them in the field. This is something that was customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We also heard testimony that while he was out there performing these tasks, there was no radio -- there was no radio available in the vehicle and no one can remember whether there was a Motorola. Could that explain also why perhaps Colonel Blagojevic wasn't at the meeting on July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think this is speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm just stating the facts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no. You're asking this witness to guess the reason why Mr. Blagojevic was there. You see, it's far beyond the ability of this witness. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honour. But also, it's really irrelevant whether we've heard testimony on something or not. This is not something that is a question for this witness. That's irrelevant as well as, I mean, Mr. Karnavas of course can argue all these things, but as the witness himself has pointed out...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please drop this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.
