As far as the relevancy with respect to the argument that allegedly ensued, I think it does go to the credibility of one of the star witnesses of the Prosecution, and that's why I thought it was relevant to delve into that, and also to perhaps give the Trial Chamber an opportunity to, you know, make a decision as to why the gentleman may not recall Colonel Blagojevic being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on the evening of the 12th, as I understand it, you received certain orders. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: On the 12th, in the evening, I did not receive any orders except for General Krstic who was told that by 8.00 on the 13th he was to prepare a decision to carry out the Zepa operation. Out of that decision, it was normal to accept -- to expect that the units would be given tasks if this decision was approved. We were just present during this act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for clarifying that. And I take it one of the reasons why you were present was so that you, as one of the commanders, or the commanders that were there might be able to provide some input as to whether that particular operation was feasible under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that's how we reacted. Yes, that's how I personally reacted, that we should not continue further operations with these forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one of the reasons was that the forces had -- were tired and needed some rest, and perhaps you wanted to get fresh troops for a -- another operation. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I take it you walked away from the meeting that evening realising that your concerns were not being listened to because afterwards you had requested General Krstic to come and personally inform the troops. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can go step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was the decision made that evening that the operation to Zepa would take place as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I've already said that. General Krstic was given the task of preparing a decision by 8.00 on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Sometimes I have to repeat the question, so don't get irritated with me. It's not for any other reason. Now, the following -- did you request that evening for anyone to address the troops regarding this new order that was going to be coming your way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Right. And as I understand it, it was General Mladic who actually came out and gave the speech to the men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that was to motivate them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it after that, the men that might have been inspired by the speech given by Mladic were not too happy to go on to Zepa. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the order remained as it was. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I'm a soldier, and the order remained, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether on that particular evening the Bratunac Brigade was also ordered -- or the next day was ordered to go to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know if the Bratunac Brigade sent a -- I believe a company with the chief of staff of the Bratunac Brigade at some point towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know about that order. But I know that at the end of the Zepa operation there were parts, or actually one unit from the Bratunac Brigade as part of the forces which were completing that process of the Zepa operation. When they arrived is something that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you indicate -- you were shown a document from your diary which reflects that -- I believe searching operations. Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And it's your understanding that upon reflection and looking at that particular note, that that notation with respect to searching was an extension or a continuation of the searching of the terrain as was requested of you as early as the morning of July 12th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would that be a proper military activity under the circumstances, searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And why so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Because the area of responsibility - I'm coming back to that - of the Bratunac and the Milici Brigade had to do with holding the lines towards the Srebrenica enclave. And it was logical to -- for that unit to continue doing the same task.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say zone of responsibility, and I want to make sure that we don't get confused because I thought we agreed earlier on that the rules do not state anything about a zone of responsibility for the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. This has been asked and answered several times. This is just repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas, I think there's no misunderstanding. We all know that. We could refer to the previous questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I just want to be on the safe side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You are safe enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me switch to another topic. On the 13th you indicated that you drove through Potocari, and you were able to see the trucks with some men or women, children, and others. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe, if I'm not mistaken, that you would have seen them as well on the 12th. Maybe not that same activity, but you would have seen some people gathered there on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Asking him to speculate what he would have seen, and that's just not a question. And given the time frame he said he went through Potocari, it doesn't really reflect the reality on the ground either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Maybe there wasn't anybody on the 12th in Potocari, if that's what this Prosecutor is suggesting. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the evening when we went through, I don't think they were loading any more. But if you want to suggest they were, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I didn't suggest they were loading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The parties should not argue in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, did you drive through Potocari on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you notice anybody in Potocari, any Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Of course that I noticed, and this is what I said earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely. That's what I was driving at. And you saw some on the 13th as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, you having -- you being in that area, part of the Drina Corps, could you please tell us who was in charge of that operation, taking care of all of those people? Was it Mladic, the Main Staff; was it Zivanovic, Krstic at some point? Was it Vidoje Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade? Who was responsible tore these people that you know of, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Which people? The ones that I saw, the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know who was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know who ordered the various police and military police to be there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: If General Mladic in the course of that meeting of the 12th in the evening talked with somebody regarding the evacuation and said that he would secure the vehicles and that the other side should secure the fuel, then I assume that everything regarding the evacuation, the assembly, and the boarding came out of that order of his, and that there was some kind of signature or something of his on that order and that there was somebody who was supposed to implement the lower orders and the activities arising out of that regarding the evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it specifically you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, specifically no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Exactly. Concretely, you don't know. All right. Now, we know from the testimony that we've had here that the men were separated and were detained and transported at some point to various detention places in Bratunac. Some remained on buses, others went to schools or other places. Do you know who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would the fact that they were in these buses and in the school in Bratunac or other facilities, would that place them under the responsibility of the Bratunac Brigade commander while at the same time you have either Mladic or Krstic and their men in and around Bratunac during that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. He said he doesn't know who is responsible, and I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- we know where this witness fits in. This could go on forever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is indeed, Your Honour. It is indeed. It is indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I hope you could move on because we don't have much time left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. It's physically impossible to finish today. But I will try to hit the high points. That's what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right, let's get on to another topic. I want to talk to you a little bit about the functions of the chief of intelligence and security. All right. I'm speaking in a general sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. At this point, that's very much beyond the scope of direct, and at this point in the trial, this exploratory mission into trying to make him a potential expert is inappropriate. We have time. He has spoken specifically on specific acts. I generally have not objected to this, because it's -- out of convenience it's easier to get this material now out of a witness than bring him back. But at this point with only this much time, an exploratory effort into expertise that's not related to his testimony is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I be heard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am deeply unmoved - unmoved - by the time. Because the Prosecutor took his time. He could have brought this witness earlier. I have been patient. I allowed them to take as long as they wanted. They chose Friday so I shouldn't be rushed at this point. Secondly, the Prosecutor went into the gentleman's background. The gentleman not only is a -- you know, has the experience and the background, but he taught this. This is a major point. This is a Prosecution witness. We've heard several Prosecution witnesses with respect to this. I'm merely trying to get into the meat and potatoes of the case. Also, when they took the gentleman's statement, when they took -- although they didn't elicit the information today, they asked him specifically about the security officer. Now, just because today they decided that tactically speaking it wasn't worth it, it doesn't mean that I can't get into it. And they certainly thought he was expert enough to elicit that information from him when they took his statement, and the question, might I add, is posed by Mr. McCloskey himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think that this Trial Chamber promised you that if in the future you need this witness, we will do our best to bring this witness back as your witness in your case. And I only allowed you to ask two questions in this area. I hope your question should be as concise as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just leave that for the next time. Because two questions, I can't guarantee it. And I don't want to violate your directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me move on to another area, sir. While you were serving with the Drina Corps and during this period of time and afterwards, did you come across any information, whether it's hearsay, third-hand, fourth-hand, who cares, that Mr. Blagojevic, Colonel Blagojevic, was directly involved in any of the atrocities that occurred after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In light of the Court's ruling, Your Honour, at this point I will stop, with the understanding that I will be bringing the gentleman back during the case in-chief. I understand that he will be making himself available, and we also need to get into his -- into the other aspects of the case that have not -- have yet to be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think you have to ask a question directly to this witness whether this witness is willing to come as your witness in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I was relying on the Court's promises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, our promise will be the last resort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, in light of some of the documents that you brought here yesterday, because they haven't been translated and because of the time, and we want to get you back home, would you be willing to come back at a later time, again, let me stress to you that your status is not going to change, but would you be willing to come back at a later time to help us out with a little bit more information in this very, very important case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: I don't know what the procedure is with respect to this possibility of testifying. But I have nothing against participating in learning the truth, or rather what happened to the best of my knowledge. I shall contribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very, very much, sir. And I apologise for this inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Colonel. I apologise, I'm going to have to look at this from this angle. The screen's in the way. But since 23 we're in closed session or, rather, private session, Your Honour, I'm going 24 to ask the witness three or four questions relating his CV,and (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can see in view of your impressive CV that you will be able to help us with respect to the application of the rules and regulation that we discussed here. If I say I'm right, that it is the duty of all superior officers to raise the flag, including the commander of the brigade in the morning hours, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us briefly all the activities in the command of your 2nd Romanija Brigade specifically, what you do in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Apart from those who were up at the front line in their positions, all the rest, which is the smaller portion of men, engage in activities as do any other armies in the world, I assume. That is to say the reveille, they get up, they wash, see to their personal hygiene, have breakfast, the flag is then raised, the flag-raising ceremony, and the regular activities that ensue and have to be accomplished during that day. During the war, meant supplies, seeing to supplies for the units and supplies of the different units from the different warehouses, store houses, providing food, clothing, footwear, and requirements of that kind. Catering to the needs of the unit generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that the morning briefings were customary where the command of the brigade would meet and assign the daily tasks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that would be after the flag-raising ceremony. And as I say, the working day would begin with this morning briefing which would mean a short meeting to hear what had happened in the meantime, since the rest period to the morning, to brief the subordinates, and if we're talking about the war period, what took place during the night, whether there were any problems up at the front line, if everybody -- and everybody would be informed of this state of affairs and the assignments given. The meetings, these briefings were very short.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you helps and give us your comments on paragraph 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I should like the usher to help us here, please, to give the colonel a copy and the other copies to be distributed to Their Honours and the Court. Your Honours, this is a document, an exhibit, it is P394, in actual fact. Exhibit P394, instructions for the work of the staffs, and this exhibit has been tendered into evidence and presented through the testimony of Mr. Richard Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let's try and comment paragraph or Rule 114 in the instructions. It states clearly here that this deals with decision-making by the commander without previous consultations with the command. And it says that in the case of sudden enemy activity in the course of combat operations when the situation changes rapidly and in other circumstances when there's not enough time to consult the command organs at all, the commander has the right and duty without consultations to make his own decisions. Am I correct in saying, Colonel, that in July 1995, the circumstances were such when many commanders were put in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, through force of circumstance, did you ever find yourself in a position of that kind, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I have a specific question. For example, the engineers unit needs to be used in your brigade or some other brigade, a situation like that occurs, for instance. We have an extraordinary situation, intensive combat operations are underway, and as this rule states, the situation changes rapidly from one moment to the next. Would you agree with me that it is quite a feasible situation in which the commander without consulting the staff officer from the engineering field takes a decision to deploy the engineers unit, his engineers unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So these, then, could be tasks as much as mining or demining the terrain, or erecting fortification or any other activities that the engineers' unit is in charge of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I'd like to move on. I won't be using that exhibit any longer. Thank you. I'm going to ask you several hypotheticals now. Let's look at some hypothetical situations which could have taken place, and then help us on the basis of the rules and give us an explanation. As brigade commander, you arrive in your unit, and at the entrance to the building of the headquarters or on the staircase, for example, somebody comes up to you from behind, a duty officer approaches you from behind, at that point in time, would it be in keeping with the rules and regulations that he, that is to say, the duty officer, speaks to you there on the staircase in the hallway? Would you stay back and hear what he has to report, or, according to the rules of conduct between a superior and his subordinate, would he have the duty of reporting to you in the duty officer's room about the events that came to pass?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: During the war, and I assume your question implies wartime, the duty officer who would otherwise be in the operations room of the headquarters or command would not go out to inform on the situation. He just got up, opened the door, and in the operations room he would inform me of the role -- of the state in the units. Now, if there was a duty officer in the brigade, not in the staff, then this duty officer at a command post in the rear or staff command or anything like that, they would receive reports outside the premises to hear how the soldiers spent the night, what tasks were accomplished and what -- which weren't, tasks not tied to the fight line and basic combat orders for the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. May I just for the transcript clarify this. So the duty operations officer cannot leave his official premises, his office, the place where he performs his duty. He can only report to you in those premises, in that room. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, I now have a question for you linked to the interview granted here by one of the accused from this case, later on after pronouncing himself. I'm talking about Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Obrenovic in actual fact. In an interview in which he granted to Mr. McCloskey, the conversation took the following lines: Mr. McCloskey asked him the following: "The decision as to the fate of those prisoners - and he meant the prisoners coming to Zvornik - was Obrenovic's decision, it was up to him." And Obrenovic says that he received information that this order had come from Mladic, and that Mr. Popovic would put it into practice, whereas I then represented the brigade commander. That's what he says. Mr. McCloskey then went on to ask him the following. He said that the decision to carry everything out, the killings in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade rested on him, Obrenovic, and that he accepted his responsibility; that is to say, that the members of his brigade participate in the killing of those people. And Obrenovic's answer to that was yes, he did accept responsibility for his brigade to take part in the killings. Now, my question to you is as follows: On the basis of the rules and regulations, would my conclusion be correct, that is, that Dragan Obrenovic by accepting responsibility for killing these men, that that would mean that his soldiers could not do that without his order, without an order from him? Would I be right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Well, without his order, or rather somebody's order, quite certainly that could not have been put into practice. That is my conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, if the brigade commander in the area of responsibility or, as we like to call it, the zone of defence, in line with the rules the brigade is at his position raising the soldiers' morale, is engaged in commanding, according to the rules, is he in the field, in the terrain, or is he considered to be present in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Present in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying, then, that from your answer I can deduce that in the list of those present in the brigade recording the presence of people in the brigade there should be a plus, meaning yes, presence in the brigade, not T, meaning on the terrain or absence or away from the brigade. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And help me out with one more point, please: If an assistant to the commander, one of the assistants to the brigade commander, that means an assistant for the rear, for example, or for intelligence or for security, for moral guidance, is at the forward command post on duty there, according to the rules is that person then considered to be present in the brigade, or is he considered to be T, in the terrain -- on the terrain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Within the frameworks of his zone or assignment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, within the area of his brigade or zone of his brigade and within his regular assignment of being on duty at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: He is considered to be present in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, let's recapitulate. So in the book of -- in the register or in the log, it would say Krstic [as interpreted] present, and there wouldn't be a capital T denoting he was outside the brigade zone on the terrain. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. When I said -- Krstic, I meant cross, not the surname Krstic. When I said Krstic, I meant small cross, not the surname Krstic. So could that be corrected, please. Thank you. And I just have a few more questions for the end. I think Mr. McCloskey would agree with me that I was right to put that right, to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, thank you. Just a few more questions, please. Bear with me. You went to your assignment, combat assignment in Srebrenica. You are outside the zone of defence of your brigade. Now, your absence from the zone, from the zone of defence of the brigade, is that registered in the corps as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: That I'm absent from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Well, if I'm with part of my unit, I'm still considered to be in the brigade, if I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The question was if you are absent, outside the zone of the brigade's defence, you've gone in the terrain, you've gone to another area with your unit, should this be registered, your absence, be registered in the corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this brings me to my next question. If you're in the terrain, in the field, and the chief of staff or deputy commander of the brigade remains in the brigade, can he now go outside the zone of the defence of the brigade without the corps command knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, in an undisciplined unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And the conclusion would be that in any disciplined unit and army, this would not be possible. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: That's right, it would not be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I have just two more questions for the end. Help me out here, please, Colonel: According to the rules, who replaces duty operations officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: The commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if there is no -- the commander is not there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Then the person who performance the duty, the deputy commander or chief of staff, if such a post exists formation-wise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In an organised and well-disciplined army as we said a moment ago, can the following happen, that this replacement or the handover between the superior duty officer and the incoming duty officer be done without the presence of the commander who is in the brigade and who says, for example, "you can replace each other yourselves," and that the duty officer can come up and receive assignments? Is that possible according to the rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: It is not usual, not customary. But as a possibility, it can happen if at the command post a superior commander has arrived and meets with him, and the commander is informed in the morning by the outgoing duty officer about the situation and at the time when the shift takes place. He will not interrupt this conversation with his superior. But once the situation has become clear, once he is clear on what has happened, then he can say "sign the documents and effect the shift." And when the man goes out, he can say "I'll call you to be more specific as to the assignments." Otherwise not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this answer of yours indicates that the commander's presence is necessary in this handover and takeover of duty. Thank you, Colonel. Now, please don't take this as a personal question, but as a hypothetical. In the zone of defence of your unit or any unit, and there are civilians who have been taken prisoner, secured by the police unit under your command and pursuant to your orders can the following happen in an organised, well-disciplined army: That a soldier or group of soldiers from that same unit of yours on his own decision kills these POWs without the knowledge of the commander of the unit? Can that happen ever?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that such a major event can only take place with the commander's knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And can this be an incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: One that the commander need not know about it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his last answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, we didn't pick up your answer for the last question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My last question was this: Is it possible for a situation of this kind to occur as an incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes, that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Without the commander's knowledge? And I think your answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-206
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any redirect, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And I would say P473, it's under seal. It's -- maybe we should go into private session if I'm going to talk about these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. The Trial Chamber has noticed that there are two outstanding issues before it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The first relates to the Prosecution's notice of filing of 92 bis statement of February 5th 2004 concerning the statement of Witness W152. The Trial Chamber made a decision before on 30th of June 2003, but the Trial Chamber further noted that it would reserve this decision concerning whether cross-examination of the witness would be required. At this stage, we would like to say that the Trial Chamber sees no reason for the cross-examination of Witness 152. This statement is admitted into the evidence and seeks to put this into the record. It is so decided. The second matter relates to the decision on the Prosecution's motion for judicial notice of adjudicated facts and documentary evidence of 19th December 2003. It's about the so-called report of the Secretary-General entitled "The Fall of Srebrenica" in which documents in Tab B of the Prosecution's motion of August 6th 2003 were admitted. Tab B relates to the documents to which all the parties agree. It has come to the notice of the Trial Chamber that the documents with 65 ter number 657, 658, which is the same report in tab B of the Prosecution's motion as well as in the tab C. These documents are objected to by the Jokic's Defence during a 65 ter Conference. Therefore, the Trial Chamber would like to seek some clarifications on this matter from the Jokic Defence. Mr. Stojanovic, are you still objecting to the admission of this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I must admit that at this point I don't have the document with me, but in view of the arguments that we stated at that time, I stand by that objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, this document is a United Nations report. It's kind of an official document. We may not agree with the views expressed in it, but this document is a very famous document. Almost everybody who knows Srebrenica knows this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. And that was not the reason why we put in our objection. After the 65 ter considerations, we said that some of the things that are stated in this document are practically counter to the facts that we have here already in the documents of the case. The question whether it was or was not demilitarised and whether there were or there were no organised military personnel in the Srebrenica zone, and finally what is the final objective, the starting and the final objective of the Krivaja 1995 operation. These are the reasons, and not the authenticity of the statement of such an eminent party such as the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I understand that this document is just about the background information, the massacre which had happened. It does not go directly to the factual conduct of your client, Mr. Jokic. I don't think his name was mentioned there at all. Of course, concerning the situations, different parties may have different views, you know. But that is not the subject matter of this very case. So this Trial Chamber will make a decision that this document is admitted into the evidence, and the Registrar could assign an exhibit number to this document. Mr. Stojanovic, I think in your case, in the Defence case, you may present any evidence you like to rebut any claims which are listed in that document and which are related to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. And I know that you are dominus litis of this procedure. I respect your decision. And after considering all the elements from the combat reports of the BH army, perhaps there won't be any need for us to deal with that when the time comes for us to present our case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Karnavas, I think yesterday you mentioned something about a scheduling order. Now, it's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. As you know, the case took a little bit longer than it had originally been told it would take. These were circumstances beyond the control of either party. We didn't object. We didn't object for the reasons that we thought it was important, to give the Prosecution every opportunity to put on their entire case. We don't object if they want to go on further. But I think they're going to be resting today. In any event, because of this additional testimony, it has been extremely difficult for us to be out there in the terrain at the same time. We do believe that we will able to get the 98 bis motion in on time, although frankly I would appreciate if we could just amend it slightly to have -- for us to be able to have it in, say, 10.00 on Tuesday morning. So I know we had three days. And frankly, I think it would be fair to start with Monday, so it is due on Wednesday. But I'm not seeking to conclude Saturday and Sunday. But If we could have until, say, Tuesday at 10.00, we will have it in. And I don't think that's going to delay anything. We do need to go out in the field. We do need to make a list of our witnesses and do all the other necessary things that are required of us, such as summary of witnesses and what have you. We believe that a more realistic date for us would be somewhere around the 16th of March to present a list of witnesses. And I can probably assure the Court that the list is going to be tentative because there probably will be -- we'll be asking for additions to that list. We believe the Prosecution has done this. We haven't objected. And I think as long as we provide adequate notice, that it's not going to interfere with the Prosecution at all. And of course, it's always subject to the Court's decision whether those witnesses would be necessary. But I just want to let you know. As far as for the actual commencement of the Defence case, thinking in -- I just read recently that Mr. Milosevic was given 150 days. Now, granted, he has got a bigger case. But then again, he has got three amici, he has got his own -- armada of his own, you know, although they are not necessarily in Court. And of course, he does have his health. So given that, I think asking for a commencement date of April 5 for us is pretty reasonable, and I think that because we also need to make an opening statement, and that's going to take some time. We got to be out in the field. So -- and I've consulted with Mr. Stojanovic, and I think he's in total agreement with us starting at that point. I don't believe that Mr. McCloskey would object. In fact, I ran it by him, and he didn't seem to express any reservations, though he might have some. I just didn't pick up on any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Stojanovic, do you agree with the submissions by Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If I may just say something, we have prepared our submissions according to 98 bis. But we need a day or two to coordinate that with the sessions of today and yesterday. It's quite understandable in view of the fact that we have to go out into the field, that the deadlines that Mr. Karnavas spoke about, the 16th in order to submit a preliminary witness list and for the beginning of trial, are not excessive, are not unrealistic. So I support what he said wholly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, which days do you think is proper for you if you want to submit your list? Or you prefer to do it at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course each wise and cautious man would try to have the date as late as possible. There's no dilemma there. But as far as the submissions are concerned, I've already said, that we have no problem with that. So objectively, our case is smaller than that of Mr. Karnavas, so it's quite understandable that my colleague Branko and I have already done most of our work by dividing up our Defence tasks. As far as the witness list is concerned, I know best what the situation is like in the field. I know where all of these people are. And if we wish to respect 65 ter, we must take their statement to see whether they will testify viva voce or via videolink or under 92 bis. So this implies for us to revisit all of those witnesses. So I propose that it is the 16th, as far as the witness list. And as far as the beginning of the trial, again, I support the 5th, as Mr. Karnavas said. Of course, reserving the right, if you permit us, that we can also perhaps provide you with a list of our witnesses after this list is provided by Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objections to the dates proposed by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I don't. I especially appreciate both Defence's indulgence in this last week. And I certainly know what it's like trying to get ready for the beginning of a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I think, you know, we are in a position to make a decision orally, and a written decision will follow concerning the scheduling order. The Defence should submit their 98 bis submissions on the 2nd of March, 4.00, before 4.00 that afternoon. And the Prosecution has ten days for the response. That will be the 12th of March before 4.00. And the Defence should submit their 65 ter submissions on the 18th of March. I have to say that it is a preliminary list which will be subject to the further discussions with the parties and with the Chamber and subject to any further changes in the future. And Defence conference will start on the 5th of April, which is the Monday, and the Defence case will start on the 6th of April, which is a Tuesday. Here, I have to remind the Defence that on the 9th to 12th will be the Easter break. We hope you could have a one-day witness as your first witness. It is so decided. A written scheduling order will be issued next week. Yes, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the record, I would like to make my position clear. I'm not convinced in the success of the next phase of my Defence, and I energetically refuse the engagement of the persons from the Defence which is imposed upon me and which I do not accept. And please, in this sense, I would like certain steps be taken in order for my confidence to be restored. It has been destroyed. And the proof of that is also the public and revised decision of the Appeals Chamber in which I can see that something is not quite right there. And some things have remained very -- as very big secrets. And I do not wish to have any secrets. I wish everything to be out in the open. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic. I think your statement is correctly reflected in the transcript. And of course, we'll send this transcript to the Appeals Chamber to see what they could do. But at this moment, for Judges in the Trial Chamber, we cannot do very much but only submit this transcript to the Appeals Chamber. Thank you. But we'll bear your concern in mind. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One question regarding the 98 bis filings, there had been some discussion about the page limit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it has been decided. Altogether 30 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Both Defence can put in 30 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: They will each have 30 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution just respond once with 60 pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think so. Well, it depends on whether you respond separately or all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to respond together. The fundamental facts don't need to be repeated but as you're aware these are two very different separate cases, so -- and I don't -- I'm sure you know by now we don't try to mount on the pages, and I certainly hope it won't be anywhere near 60, but....

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So could I regard this for an application for explanation of pages on your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's only fair that -- yes, if that's the way you want to consider it, but if they can both -- two separate motions with 30 each, we should be able to respond in kind to what they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Since there are many issues common, common issues in both cases, so I don't think you can have 60 pages. We'll give you 45 pages altogether. Thank you. Mr. McCloskey, could I regard that this is the last witness for your case, and you will rest for your case from this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one last matter, and I haven't raised this before, but are we going to be allowed to present oral argument on the 98 bis motion? I know that some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think so. It's not the European practice, it's not the European practice unless you specifically request and there is a reason behind it. Generally speaking, not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I know that other Trial Chambers allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So I declare that the Prosecution's case is closed. And the hearing is adjourned.
